source.title: The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, Volume 1
source.attribution: Edward Gibbon, The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, Volume 1, Project Gutenberg, public domain

cards.title: Augustus stopped conquering once more land was bringing more risk than reward
cards.body:
For seven centuries Rome had grown by conquest. Augustus, who ruled from 27 BC to AD 14, chose to stop. Gibbon explains his reasoning: distant wars were getting harder, their outcome less certain and the new lands less worth holding. Instead of marching against the Parthians, in what is now Iran and Iraq, he negotiated, and by an honourable treaty won back the legionary standards and prisoners that Crassus had lost decades before.

Most of his successors kept his rule of holding the frontiers rather than pushing them. The lesson travels well: past a certain size, each new expansion costs more and protects less. Knowing when growth has stopped paying is a skill in itself.
cards.quote: it was reserved for Augustus to relinquish the ambitious design of subduing the whole earth, and to introduce a spirit of moderation into the public councils.
cards.locator: Chapter I: The Extent Of The Empire In The Age Of The Antonines—Part I ¶4
cards.apply_it: List one project, client or commitment that has grown beyond what it gives back. Decide whether to hold it where it is instead of expanding it.

quiz.question: How did Augustus recover the standards Crassus had lost to the Parthians?
options: By a great invasion of Parthia
By paying a ransom in gold
quiz.explanation: Gibbon says Augustus avoided risking his legions and won back the standards and prisoners by treaty.

cards.title: Augustus learned from Caesar's murder that names matter as much as power
cards.body:
Julius Caesar was killed in 44 BC partly, Gibbon argues, because he flaunted his power and let people think he wanted to be king. His adopted heir Octavian, later called Augustus, drew the opposite lesson. He kept the old republican offices, the senate and the familiar titles, and gathered real control quietly behind them. Romans accepted a monarchy as long as it was called something else.

Gibbon calls this a mask, and he is not admiring. But the observation is sharp: people react to names and symbols, not just to substance. Today a 'restructuring' and a 'layoff' can be the same event. Notice when a gentle label is doing the work of hiding a hard reality, whether others use it or you do.
cards.quote: Augustus was sensible that mankind is governed by names; nor was he deceived in his expectation, that the senate and people would submit to slavery, provided they were respectfully assured that they still enjoyed their ancient freedom.
cards.locator: Chapter III: The Constitution In The Age Of The Antonines.—Part II ¶3
cards.apply_it: Next time you read an announcement at work or in the news, rewrite its key sentence in the plainest words you can. What changes?

quiz.question: Why, according to Gibbon, did Augustus avoid the title of king?
options: He thought it was beneath him
The senate had given it to someone else
The title had helped turn Romans against Caesar
The army refused to accept it
quiz.explanation: Caesar provoked his fate by the show of power; the title of king armed Romans against him, so Augustus ruled under old republican names.

cards.title: Rome's wiser emperors shared power with their heirs before they died
cards.body:
Rome had no fixed rule of succession, so an emperor's death was a dangerous moment. The armies might back a rival, and civil war could follow. Gibbon describes how careful rulers closed that gap. Augustus gave his adopted son Tiberius powers equal to his own over the provinces and armies. Vespasian made his son Titus, a popular general whose ambitions some suspected, a full partner in government, and Titus served him faithfully.

The heir was already doing the job when the old ruler died, so the change of master was barely felt. Any team or family business faces the same risk. A successor who has already been doing the work is the best insurance against chaos.
cards.quote: In elective monarchies, the vacancy of the throne is a moment big with danger and mischief.
cards.locator: Chapter III: The Constitution In The Age Of The Antonines.—Part II ¶13
cards.apply_it: Pick one task that only you know how to do. This week, walk someone else through it so they could carry it on without you.

quiz.question: How did Vespasian handle his son Titus, whose designs some people suspected?
options: He gave Titus's army to another general
He kept him far from the legions
He made him a full partner in imperial power
quiz.explanation: Instead of listening to suspicion, Vespasian shared full imperial powers with Titus, who proved a faithful partner.

cards.title: Nerva passed over his relatives and chose the best man for the job
cards.body:
In AD 96 the cruel emperor Domitian was murdered and the elderly senator Nerva took his place. Nerva was gentle and respected, but he soon saw that he was too old and weak to control the disorder around him. Although he had relatives, he adopted an outsider: Trajan, a capable general of about forty who commanded the army on the lower Rhine. Trajan became one of Rome's most admired rulers. Gibbon notes that more than 250 years after Trajan's death, the senate still wished each new emperor the luck of Augustus and the virtue of Trajan.

Nerva's greatest act was admitting his own limits. Choosing the strongest candidate instead of the closest one takes humility, and it can outlast everything else you do.
cards.quote: Though he had several relations, he fixed his choice on a stranger.
cards.locator: Chapter III: The Constitution In The Age Of The Antonines.—Part II ¶19
cards.apply_it: If you are hiring, promoting or choosing a partner, write down the criteria before you look at the names. Then check your choice against them.

quiz.question: Why did Nerva adopt Trajan as his successor?
options: He saw that his age left him unable to control the disorder
quiz.explanation: Gibbon says Nerva's feeble age could not stem the public disorder, so he chose a vigorous outsider.

cards.title: Trajan chased Alexander's fame, and his eastern conquests did not last
cards.body:
Trajan, emperor from AD 98 to 117, broke with Augustus's policy of restraint. After conquering Dacia, in what is now Romania, he marched east against the Parthians. He sailed down the Tigris to the Persian Gulf and, Gibbon says, sighed that he was too old to equal Alexander the Great. Kings sent homage and the senate heard of new provinces almost daily.

Then Trajan died, and his successor soon gave the eastern conquests up. Gibbon blames a world that applauds destroyers more loudly than benefactors. The question for us is whose applause we are working for. Goals chosen to match someone else's legend can cost a great deal and leave little behind.
cards.quote: as long as mankind shall continue to bestow more liberal applause on their destroyers than on their benefactors, the thirst of military glory will ever be the vice of the most exalted characters.
cards.locator: Chapter I: The Extent Of The Empire In The Age Of The Antonines—Part I ¶30
cards.apply_it: Think of a goal you are chasing mainly to impress others. Write one sentence on what it would give you if nobody ever heard about it.

quiz.question: Whose fame did Trajan hope to equal?
quiz.explanation: Gibbon says the praises of Alexander kindled a dangerous emulation in Trajan, who regretted he was too old to match him.

cards.title: Hadrian gave back Trajan's conquests rather than defend what he could not hold
cards.body:
Romans believed their borders would never shrink. A legend said the boundary god Terminus had refused to give way even to Jupiter. Yet in AD 117 the first act of the new emperor Hadrian was to give up Trajan's eastern conquests in Armenia, Mesopotamia and Assyria. He withdrew the garrisons and made the Euphrates the frontier again, as Augustus had advised.

Critics said he was jealous of Trajan. Gibbon thinks prudence is the likelier motive, and a long peace followed. Pulling back from a position you cannot hold looks like defeat, and pride makes it hard. But hanging on only because you have already paid for something is how small losses become large ones.
cards.quote: The resignation of all the eastern conquests of Trajan was the first measure of his reign.
cards.locator: Chapter I: The Extent Of The Empire In The Age Of The Antonines.—Part II ¶1
cards.apply_it: Name one commitment you keep mainly because you have already invested in it. Ask: if I were starting today, would I take it on?

quiz.question: Which river did Hadrian restore as the eastern frontier?
quiz.explanation: Following the advice of Augustus, Hadrian withdrew from Trajan's eastern provinces and set the frontier on the Euphrates.

cards.title: Rome grew strong by welcoming talent that Athens and Sparta shut out
cards.body:
Athens and Sparta guarded their citizenship jealously, and Gibbon notes that the number of Athenian citizens actually shrank. Rome did the opposite. It steadily granted citizenship to allies, provincials and people who served it. By the age of the Antonines, in the second century AD, the grandsons of Gauls who had fought Julius Caesar commanded legions and sat in the senate, and Spain had given Rome the emperor Trajan.

Gibbon's point is that people allowed to rise become defenders of a system rather than rebels against it. Teams, firms and countries that let newcomers earn a real stake tend to draw in more energy than those that keep the door shut.
cards.quote: The aspiring genius of Rome sacrificed vanity to ambition, and deemed it more prudent, as well as honorable, to adopt virtue and merit for her own wheresoever they were found, among slaves or strangers, enemies or barbarians.
cards.locator: Chapter II: The Internal Prosperity In The Age Of The Antonines.—Part I ¶30
cards.apply_it: Look at who gets promoted or heard in a group you belong to. Is someone talented being kept on the outside? Find one way to bring them in.

quiz.question: What happened to the number of Athenian citizens during the city's most flourishing era?
quiz.explanation: Gibbon contrasts Athens, whose citizen body shrank from about thirty to twenty-one thousand, with Rome's steadily growing citizenship.

cards.title: Many faiths lived side by side in Rome because none was forced on the others
cards.body:
In the second century AD the Roman world held a great many gods and cults, from Egypt to Britain. Gibbon describes a broad tolerance: the empire let each people keep the worship of its ancestors, and the cults rarely quarrelled. His famous sentence sums up how three groups saw it: the ordinary worshipper, the sceptical philosopher and the practical official.

Gibbon's wit is aimed at all three, and his picture is rosier than the full record, since Rome did at times punish groups it saw as a threat. Still, the core point holds. Where no single creed is imposed by force, neighbours of different beliefs can live together in peace, and that remains one of history's hard-won lessons.
cards.quote: The various modes of worship, which prevailed in the Roman world, were all considered by the people, as equally true; by the philosopher, as equally false; and by the magistrate, as equally useful.
cards.locator: Chapter II: The Internal Prosperity In The Age Of The Antonines.—Part I ¶5
cards.apply_it: Have a curious, non-argumentative conversation this week with someone whose beliefs differ from yours. Ask what their faith or philosophy gives them.

quiz.question: According to Gibbon, how did the Roman magistrate regard the various religions?
quiz.explanation: The people saw them as equally true, the philosopher as equally false, and the magistrate as equally useful.

cards.title: Rome feared its silk trade would bankrupt it, but the silver never ran out
cards.body:
Every summer, Gibbon reports, about 120 ships sailed from Egypt's Red Sea coast to India and Sri Lanka, riding the monsoon winds, and came back with silk, pearls, gems and spices. A pound of silk was said to be worth a pound of gold. Because eastern merchants wanted little from Rome except silver, senators complained that the empire's wealth was being given away for luxuries.

Gibbon tested the complaint. Comparing the values of gold and silver over time, he found silver had become more plentiful, not scarcer: the mines more than covered the trade. Fears about money vanishing appear in every age. Before panicking about a trend, look for a number that would show whether it is really happening.
cards.quote: Such was the style of discontent, brooding over the dark prospect of approaching poverty.
cards.locator: Chapter II: The Internal Prosperity In The Age Of The Antonines. Part IV ¶20
cards.apply_it: Pick one money worry you have. Find the actual figure behind it this week, such as a balance, a price trend or a bill total, before deciding what to do.

quiz.question: How did Gibbon test the claim that eastern trade was draining Rome's silver?
options: By counting ships in Egyptian ports
By comparing the values of gold and silver over time
quiz.explanation: Silver had grown more common relative to gold, so the trade had not exhausted Rome's wealth.

cards.title: Gibbon saw the seeds of decline inside Rome's long, comfortable peace
cards.body:
The second century was prosperous and calm, and those living through it saw no danger. Gibbon looks deeper. With one government ruling everyone and no threats nearby, the provinces lost the habit of running their own affairs and defending themselves. Spain, Gaul, Britain and the Balkans still produced brave soldiers, but ordinary citizens left their defence to a paid army and their decisions to a distant emperor. The ambitious drifted to the court, and local life sank into private indifference.

Comfort is not the problem, but skills and courage that are never used fade away. A long easy stretch is a good time to keep practising the abilities you would need if life got hard.
cards.quote: This long peace, and the uniform government of the Romans, introduced a slow and secret poison into the vitals of the empire.
cards.locator: Chapter II: The Internal Prosperity In The Age Of The Antonines. Part IV ¶32
cards.apply_it: Choose one skill you have let slip because life is easy right now, such as cooking, budgeting or fitness. Practise it for twenty minutes this week.

quiz.question: What did Gibbon call the effect of the long peace on the empire?
quiz.explanation: He argued that peace and uniform government dulled public courage and independence until the military spirit evaporated.

cards.title: Antoninus Pius ruled so calmly that history found little to say about him
cards.body:
Antoninus Pius ruled from AD 138 to 161. Gibbon compares him with Numa, the legendary peaceful king of early Rome, except that Antoninus kept order across most of the known world rather than among a few villages. His reign left few dramatic events behind, and Gibbon turns that into one of his most quoted lines about what history usually records.

In private, Gibbon says, Antoninus was kind, unpretentious and cheerful, and enjoyed his good fortune in moderation. We tend to notice leaders, managers and parents when something goes wrong. Those who quietly keep things calm and fair rarely make headlines, and that quiet is often the best sign of their success.
cards.quote: His reign is marked by the rare advantage of furnishing very few materials for history; which is, indeed, little more than the register of the crimes, follies, and misfortunes of mankind.
cards.locator: Chapter III: The Constitution In The Age Of The Antonines.—Part II ¶34
cards.apply_it: Thank someone this week whose steady, unglamorous work keeps things running smoothly for you.

quiz.question: Why did the reign of Antoninus Pius provide few materials for history?
options: It was peaceful and well ordered
Its records were lost in a fire
He banned historians from his court
It lasted only a few months
quiz.explanation: History, Gibbon says, mostly records crimes, follies and misfortunes, and Antoninus's reign had few of them.

cards.title: Marcus Aurelius held himself to strict standards and forgave others easily
cards.body:
Marcus Aurelius, emperor from AD 161 to 180, took up Stoic philosophy at the age of twelve. Gibbon says his virtue was earned through long study, and that he wrote his Meditations amid military camps. He detested war, yet spent eight winters fighting on the frozen Danube frontier when defence required it, and the hardship wore down his health. When the general Avidius Cassius rebelled and then died, Marcus regretted losing the chance to turn an enemy into a friend.

Most of us do the reverse: we excuse ourselves and judge others harshly. Marcus's rule is worth trying. Be demanding of your own conduct, patient with other people's flaws and fair to everyone.
cards.quote: He was severe to himself, indulgent to the imperfections of others, just and beneficent to all mankind.
cards.locator: Chapter III: The Constitution In The Age Of The Antonines.—Part II ¶36
cards.apply_it: Today, when someone irritates you, give them the excuse you would give yourself. When you slip, hold yourself to the standard you would set for them.

quiz.question: What did Marcus regret about the death of the rebel Avidius Cassius?
options: That he could not punish him in public
Losing the chance to turn an enemy into a friend
That the senate acted without him
quiz.explanation: Gibbon says Marcus regretted being denied the pleasure of converting an enemy into a friend, and he restrained the senate against Cassius's followers.

cards.title: Gibbon named AD 96 to 180 the happiest period in human history
cards.body:
Gibbon's most famous judgement covers the years from the death of Domitian in AD 96 to the accession of Commodus in 180. Under Nerva, Trajan, Hadrian, Antoninus Pius and Marcus Aurelius, a vast empire was governed by absolute power, but power used with wisdom and restraint. These rulers kept the forms of civil government, delighted in the image of liberty and saw themselves as answerable to the laws.

Historians today question the claim, since enslaved people, the poor and conquered peoples might have judged differently. But Gibbon's reasoning is worth noticing. He credits the age not to wealth or conquest but to the character of those in charge, and to their choice to limit themselves when no one could force them.
cards.quote: If a man were called to fix the period in the history of the world, during which the condition of the human race was most happy and prosperous, he would, without hesitation, name that which elapsed from the death of Domitian to the accession of Commodus.
cards.locator: Chapter III: The Constitution In The Age Of The Antonines.—Part II ¶44
cards.apply_it: Think of a place where you hold power over others, as a parent, manager or senior colleague. Name one limit you could choose to respect even though no one enforces it.

quiz.question: Whose accession ended Gibbon's 'most happy and prosperous' period?
quiz.explanation: The period runs from the death of Domitian in AD 96 to the accession of Commodus in 180.

cards.title: A golden age that rests on one good ruler can end with one bad one
cards.body:
Gibbon follows his praise of the Antonine age with a warning. The good emperors, he suggests, must have known that the happiness they created depended on one man's character. The senate and the laws could display a good ruler's virtues but never correct a bad one's vices, and there would always be flatterers ready to serve. Rome had already lived through Tiberius, Caligula, Nero and Domitian, and soon after Marcus came Commodus.

Organisations face the same danger. If everything good depends on one founder, boss or star, the good fortune is borrowed. Lasting strength comes from rules, habits and checks that still work when the best person leaves.
cards.quote: They must often have recollected the instability of a happiness which depended on the character of single man.
cards.locator: Chapter III: The Constitution In The Age Of The Antonines.—Part II ¶45
cards.apply_it: Identify one thing at work or at home that only works because of one person. Write down the steps so it could survive without them.

quiz.question: What weakness did Gibbon see in the happy age of the Antonines?
options: It depended on the character of one man
quiz.explanation: The senate and laws could not restrain a bad emperor, so the age's happiness hung on whoever held absolute power.

cards.title: Marcus Aurelius gave his teenage son full power, and Rome paid for it
cards.body:
Marcus Aurelius chose his own son Commodus to succeed him, instead of adopting the best man available as the emperors before him had done. Gibbon grants that Marcus tried hard: he surrounded the boy with good and learned teachers. But a grave lesson from a philosopher, Gibbon says, could be wiped out in a moment by a whisper from a bad companion. Worse, Marcus made Commodus a full partner in power at fourteen or fifteen. He lived only four more years, long enough to regret it, and Commodus became sole ruler in AD 180.

Love can blind even the wisest people. Handing someone authority before they have shown they can handle it rarely helps them, however well meant.
cards.quote: The distasteful lesson of a grave philosopher was, in a moment, obliterated by the whisper of a profligate favorite
cards.locator: Chapter IV: The Cruelty, Follies And Murder Of Commodus.—Part I ¶10
cards.apply_it: Before you hand someone new responsibility, ask what they have already shown they can manage. Give them the next step, not the whole staircase.

quiz.question: At about what age did Marcus make Commodus a full partner in imperial power?
quiz.explanation: Admitting Commodus to full power so young raised him above the restraint of reason and authority, as Marcus came to regret.

cards.title: Commodus trusted a favourite precisely because he owed everything to him
cards.body:
Commodus left government to favourites. The most notorious, Cleander, had come to Rome as a slave and rose to command the Praetorian Guard. Gibbon explains the logic: a suspicious ruler promotes people with no other base, expecting loyalty from their dependence. Cleander sold senate seats and consulships, shared the spoils of the provinces with governors, and let rich criminals buy their way out of justice. When riots broke out over a grain shortage blamed on him, Commodus had him killed to calm the crowd.

Dependence is not the same as loyalty. Promoting people for their gratitude rather than their ability invites exactly the abuses Rome suffered.
cards.quote: Suspicious princes often promote the last of mankind, from a vain persuasion, that those who have no dependence, except on their favor, will have no attachment, except to the person of their benefactor.
cards.locator: Chapter IV: The Cruelty, Follies And Murder Of Commodus.—Part I ¶35
cards.apply_it: Look at the people you rely on most. For each, ask: do I trust them because they are good at this, or because they owe me?

quiz.question: How did Cleander's power come to an end?
options: He retired rich to the provinces
Commodus had him killed after riots over grain
The senate sent him into exile
quiz.explanation: A corn monopoly blamed on Cleander set off riots, and Commodus ordered his head thrown to the people.

cards.title: Commodus ruled by fear until the people closest to him feared him most
cards.body:
In his last years Commodus put many senators to death on suspicion, especially anyone linked to the family of the Antonines, and he turned even on the servants of his own pleasures. That proved fatal. His mistress Marcia, his chamberlain Eclectus and the Praetorian prefect Laetus decided they would be next. At the end of AD 192 Marcia gave him poisoned wine, and a young wrestler finished the deed. He had ruled for thirteen years.

Gibbon marvels at how easily one hated man was removed. Power built on fear makes everyone nearby calculate their own survival. People who feel safe around a leader protect them; people who feel threatened look for a way out.
cards.quote: He had shed with impunity the noblest blood of Rome: he perished as soon as he was dreaded by his own domestics.
cards.locator: Chapter IV: The Cruelty, Follies And Murder Of Commodus.—Part II ¶25
cards.apply_it: Think about how people close to you feel when they bring you bad news. What one thing could you do to make honesty feel safer?

quiz.question: Who plotted the death of Commodus?
options: His mistress, his chamberlain and the Praetorian prefect
quiz.explanation: Marcia, Eclectus and Laetus acted because they feared they would be his next victims.

cards.title: Pertinax inherited an empty treasury and chose honesty over easy money
cards.body:
When Commodus died, the new emperor Pertinax, an elderly general and senator, found only about eight thousand pounds in the treasury, by Gibbon's reckoning. Yet he abolished the oppressive taxes Commodus had invented and cancelled the treasury's unjust claims. He halved palace spending, auctioned the court's luxuries, paid honest creditors and long-overdue wages, removed restrictions on trade, and offered unfarmed land free of tax for ten years to anyone who would cultivate it.

Gibbon says he treated economy and hard work as the true sources of wealth. When money is short, the tempting move is to squeeze harder. Cutting waste and paying what you owe builds trust that lasts longer.
cards.quote: that he was better satisfied to administer a poor republic with innocence, than to acquire riches by the ways of tyranny and dishonor.
cards.locator: Chapter IV: The Cruelty, Follies And Murder Of Commodus.—Part II ¶43
cards.apply_it: Go through last month's spending and cut one cost that brings you nothing. Put the saving towards something you owe.

quiz.question: What did Pertinax do with the luxuries of Commodus's court?
options: He sold them at public auction
He kept them for his family
He gave them to the army
He sent them to the provinces
quiz.explanation: Gold and silver plate, chariots and silk wardrobes were auctioned to help refill the treasury.

cards.title: Pertinax was murdered after 86 days for restoring discipline too quickly
cards.body:
Pertinax won the love of the people, but the Praetorian Guard, the elite troops stationed in Rome, resented him. They feared the strict discipline he meant to restore and missed the easy life under Commodus. Their prefect Laetus, who had helped make him emperor, found that Pertinax would reward a servant but would not be ruled by one. On 28 March AD 193, just eighty-six days after Commodus died, a few hundred soldiers marched on the palace. Pertinax went out to face them and reminded them of their oath, but they killed him.

Good reforms still need allies. Those who lose privileges will resist, so a reformer must build support before pulling every lever at once.
cards.quote: his new emperor would reward a servant, but would not be ruled by a favorite.
cards.locator: Chapter IV: The Cruelty, Follies And Murder Of Commodus.—Part II ¶50
cards.apply_it: Planning a change? List who loses something from it, and talk to at least one of them before you start.

quiz.question: How long did Pertinax reign?
quiz.explanation: He was killed on 28 March AD 193, eighty-six days after the death of Commodus.

cards.title: In AD 193 the Praetorian Guard sold the Roman Empire to the highest bidder
cards.body:
After killing Pertinax, the Praetorian Guard did something shocking even by Roman standards. Two men wanted the throne: Sulpicianus, Pertinax's father-in-law, and Didius Julianus, a wealthy senator. The soldiers announced from their camp walls that the empire would go to whoever paid most. Messengers carried bids back and forth until Julianus promised each soldier 6,250 drachmas and the gates opened to him.

Gibbon calls the Guard's licence the first symptom and cause of Rome's decline. Julianus spent a sleepless first night and lasted sixty-six days before the senate condemned him. Authority that can simply be bought commands no respect, and it can always be bought again by someone else.
cards.quote: proclaimed that the Roman world was to be disposed of to the best bidder by public auction.
cards.locator: Chapter V: Sale Of The Empire To Didius Julianus.—Part I ¶15
cards.apply_it: Ask yourself where in your life loyalty is being bought rather than earned. What would earning it look like?

quiz.question: How long did Didius Julianus reign after buying the empire?
quiz.explanation: Severus marched on Rome, the guards abandoned Julianus, and the senate had him executed after sixty-six days.

cards.title: Severus tore down Byzantium's walls and left the empire weaker for it
cards.body:
Septimius Severus, commander of the army on the middle Danube, marched on Rome in AD 193, took the throne, and then defeated his rivals Pescennius Niger in the east and Clodius Albinus in the west. Byzantium, today's Istanbul, stayed loyal to Niger through a three-year siege. When famine finally forced it to surrender, Severus had its magistrates and soldiers killed, its walls demolished and its privileges removed.

The historian Dio, Gibbon notes, blamed this revenge for stripping Rome of its strongest defence on the straits, and in the next century Gothic fleets sailed through. Punishing an opponent by destroying something valuable can wreck something you will need yourself.
cards.quote: The truth of this observation was but too well justified in the succeeding age, when the Gothic fleets covered the Euxine, and passed through the undefined Bosphorus into the centre of the Mediterranean.
cards.locator: Chapter V: Sale Of The Empire To Didius Julianus.—Part II ¶29
cards.apply_it: Before you retaliate after a conflict, ask what you would lose too. Is there a response that settles it without burning a bridge you need?

quiz.question: How long did Byzantium hold out against Severus?
quiz.explanation: Byzantium resisted for three years and surrendered only to famine.

cards.title: Severus spoiled his soldiers, then wondered why they no longer obeyed
cards.body:
Once in power, Severus loosened the army's discipline out of gratitude and policy. He let soldiers wear gold rings and live with their wives in their quarters, raised their pay beyond any earlier level, and taught them to expect bonuses on every occasion. Officers competed in luxury. The troops grew soft, burdensome to the provinces and impatient of command.

Severus did write to one general urging that reform begin with the officers, since an officer who loses respect will never be obeyed. Gibbon adds that the real root was the emperor's own indulgence. Rewards can strengthen a team, but rewards given to buy goodwill soon become rights that people demand.
cards.quote: the officer who has forfeited the esteem, will never command the obedience, of his soldiers.
cards.locator: Chapter V: Sale Of The Empire To Didius Julianus.—Part II ¶45
cards.apply_it: Check whether any perk you give, at work or at home, has turned from a reward into an expectation. Could you tie it to effort again?

quiz.question: Where did Severus say the reform of the army should begin?
quiz.explanation: In a surviving letter he urged a general to start the reformation with the tribunes, because officers who lose esteem cannot command obedience.

cards.title: Severus reached the top and found it worth far less than the climb
cards.body:
Septimius Severus rose from a modest start in North Africa to rule the Roman world for eighteen years. He beat every rival and left the empire at peace. Yet near the end, old and ill, he summed up his life in a sentence Gibbon quotes from the ancient sources: he had been all things, and all was of little value. Gibbon's comment is that climbing can absorb an active mind, but holding the summit never satisfies an ambitious one. Severus died at York in AD 211, his last hope pinned on two quarrelling sons.

Reaching a goal rarely feels the way we imagine. It is worth asking, while there is still time, what you really hope the climb will give you.
cards.quote: but the possession of a throne could never yet afford a lasting satisfaction to an ambitious mind.
cards.locator: Chapter VI: Death Of Severus, Tyranny Of Caracalla, Usurpation Of Marcinus.—Part I ¶2
cards.apply_it: Write down a goal you are working towards. Under it, write what you hope it will make you feel, and one way you could feel that sooner.

quiz.question: Where did Septimius Severus die?
quiz.explanation: He died at York in AD 211, in the eighteenth year of his reign, during his campaign in Britain.

cards.title: Caracalla murdered his brother and could not escape the memory
cards.body:
Severus left the empire to both his sons, Caracalla and Geta, who hated each other. In AD 211 Caracalla agreed to meet Geta in their mother's rooms to make peace, and hidden centurions killed Geta as she tried to shield him. Caracalla then bought the army's support with his father's treasure. Gibbon reports that some twenty thousand people accused of being Geta's friends were put to death.

Yet Caracalla admitted he often saw his father and brother rising to accuse him. Instead of trying to make amends, he tried to erase every reminder of Geta, which only spread the cruelty. Guilt that is buried rather than faced does not fade; it tends to drive more harm.
cards.quote: Neither business, nor pleasure, nor flattery, could defend Caracalla from the stings of a guilty conscience
cards.locator: Chapter VI: Death Of Severus, Tyranny Of Caracalla, Usurpation Of Marcinus.—Part I ¶40
cards.apply_it: Is there something you regret that you have tried to bury rather than repair? Consider one small step towards making it right.

quiz.question: How did Caracalla respond to his guilt over Geta's death?
options: He built a temple in Geta's honour
He tried to wipe out every reminder of his brother
He confessed publicly to the senate
quiz.explanation: Gibbon says his repentance only prompted him to remove whatever recalled his crime, including anyone who mourned or mentioned Geta.

cards.title: Caracalla made almost everyone a citizen, chiefly so he could tax them
cards.body:
In AD 212 Caracalla extended Roman citizenship to almost all free people in the empire. It sounds generous, and it is often remembered that way. Gibbon sees a money motive. Citizens paid a tax on inheritances and legacies, set by Augustus at one twentieth. Caracalla needed revenue for the huge rewards he lavished on the army. So he made the provincials citizens, doubled the tax to one tenth, and kept collecting their old provincial tributes as well.

Citizenship had once been a prize that opened the way to honours; forced on everyone, it became a bill. When a benefit arrives with no obvious reason, it is worth asking who will pay for it.
cards.quote: the reluctant provincials were compelled to assume the vain title, and the real obligations, of Roman citizens.
cards.locator: Chapter VI: Death Of Severus, Tyranny Of Caracalla, Usurpation Of Marcinus.—Part IV ¶56
cards.apply_it: Next time you are offered a free upgrade or new status, read the terms and find what it costs you in fees, data or obligations.

quiz.question: What did Caracalla do to the tax on inheritances and legacies?
options: Doubled it from a twentieth to a tenth
quiz.explanation: Not content with the old rate, he exacted a tenth instead of a twentieth; the old rate returned after his death.

cards.title: Alexander Severus built a day of work, study, exercise and good company
cards.body:
Alexander Severus became emperor as a teenager in AD 222, guided by his mother Julia Mamaea and wise advisers such as the jurist Ulpian. Gibbon admires his daily routine. He rose early and began with private devotion. He spent the morning in council on public business, then kept time for poetry, history and philosophy. Exercise and a bath came next, then letters and petitions until a plain supper with a few learned friends.

His thirteen years of rule brought lighter taxes and calmer provinces, though in AD 235 mutinous soldiers killed him. His day is still a fine model: serious work first, then learning, movement, correspondence and good company.
cards.quote: The dryness of business was relieved by the charms of literature; and a portion of time was always set apart for his favorite studies of poetry, history, and philosophy.
cards.locator: Chapter VI: Death Of Severus, Tyranny Of Caracalla, Usurpation Of Marcinus.—Part III ¶27
cards.apply_it: Sketch your ideal weekday with blocks for focused work, learning, movement and people. Try following it for just one day.

quiz.question: Who was constantly invited to Alexander's supper table?
quiz.explanation: His table was frugal and his guests were a few men of learning and virtue, among whom Ulpian was always invited.

cards.title: Maximin's cruelty grew out of his fear of being looked down on
cards.body:
In AD 235 the soldiers killed Alexander and made Maximin emperor. He was a giant peasant soldier from Thrace, in today's Bulgaria and northern Greece, who had risen from the ranks and was loved by the troops. Gibbon contrasts him with earlier tyrants like Nero, who were spoiled by growing up in luxury. Maximin's cruelty came from another source: the fear of contempt. He remembered being turned away from rich men's doors, and he put to death not only those who had snubbed him but even friends who had helped him, because they knew where he came from.

Insecurity becomes dangerous when it gains power. Making peace with your own story protects the people around you.
cards.quote: The cruelty of Maximin was derived from a different source, the fear of contempt.
cards.locator: Chapter VII: Tyranny Of Maximin, Rebellion, Civil Wars, Death Of Maximin.—Part I ¶15
cards.apply_it: Notice when you feel defensive about where you came from or what you lack. Pause and ask whether anyone is actually judging you.

quiz.question: Besides those who had snubbed him, whom did Maximin put to death?
options: Friends who had helped him when he was poor
quiz.explanation: Both those who had spurned and those who had protected him shared the same 'crime': they knew his humble origins.

cards.title: A slighted Parthian officer founded the Persian empire that challenged Rome
cards.body:
Rome's great eastern rival changed hands in the 220s AD. Ardashir, whom Gibbon calls Artaxerxes, had served with distinction in the army of Artabanus, the last Parthian king. Gibbon writes that royal ingratitude drove him into exile and rebellion. Ardashir defeated the Parthians in three great battles, killed Artabanus, and was hailed as King of Kings in an assembly at Balkh, in today's Afghanistan, founding the Sasanian dynasty.

His enemies said his father was a common soldier; his supporters claimed royal blood. Either way, a capable man pushed aside became the force that toppled his master. Talent that is overlooked or mistreated does not disappear. It often goes on to compete with you.
cards.quote: it appears that he was driven into exile and rebellion by royal ingratitude, the customary reward for superior merit.
cards.locator: Chapter VIII: State Of Persia And Restoration Of The Monarchy.—Part I ¶9
cards.apply_it: Think of someone whose good work you have not properly recognised. Tell them specifically what they did well this week.

quiz.question: What drove Ardashir to rebel, according to Gibbon?
quiz.explanation: Gibbon says he was driven into exile and rebellion by royal ingratitude, 'the customary reward for superior merit'.

cards.title: Decius knew a ruler's favour gives power, but only respect gives authority
cards.body:
Decius, emperor from AD 249 to 251, spent most of his short reign fighting Gothic invaders on the lower Danube. Even in the middle of the war, Gibbon says, he tried to understand why Rome was declining, and concluded that it needed public virtue, old principles and respect for the law restored. He revived the ancient office of censor, the guardian of public morals. Rather than appoint someone himself, he let the senate choose, and it named Valerian, a future emperor.

Decius died fighting the Goths soon after, so the plan came to little. But the distinction behind it lasts: a title can be handed out, but people only truly follow those they respect.
cards.quote: Conscious that the favor of the sovereign may confer power, but that the esteem of the people can alone bestow authority, he submitted the choice of the censor to the unbiased voice of the senate.
cards.locator: Chapter X: Emperors Decius, Gallus, Æmilianus, Valerian And Gallienus.—Part II ¶13
cards.apply_it: Think of one person you need to lead or influence. What have you done lately to earn their respect, rather than relying on your title?

quiz.question: How was the new censor chosen under Decius?
options: The senate chose him by vote
quiz.explanation: Decius left the choice to the senate, which unanimously named Valerian.

cards.title: Gibbon doubted the most lurid tale told about a captured Roman emperor
cards.body:
In AD 260 the emperor Valerian met the Persian king Shapur I near Edessa, in today's south-east Turkey. Misled by a bad minister and weakened by famine and disease, his army was trapped. Valerian went to negotiate and was taken prisoner, the only Roman emperor ever captured by a foreign enemy. Later writers told dramatic stories: that Shapur used him as a step to mount his horse, and that his stuffed skin was kept in a Persian temple.

Gibbon reports the tale, then questions it. The letters supporting it were forgeries, and such public humiliation of a fellow king seemed unlikely. What is certain is that Valerian died in captivity. When a story fits a moral too neatly, check it before passing it on.
cards.quote: The voice of history, which is often little more than the organ of hatred or flattery, reproaches Sapor with a proud abuse of the rights of conquest.
cards.locator: Chapter X: Emperors Decius, Gallus, Æmilianus, Valerian And Gallienus.—Part IV ¶33
cards.apply_it: Before you share a shocking story this week, find its original source. If you can't, say so when you pass it on.

quiz.question: Why did Gibbon doubt the story of Valerian's humiliation?
quiz.explanation: He calls the eastern princes' letters to Shapur manifest forgeries and finds the public degradation of a king improbable.

cards.title: Gallienus was good at everything except the job he actually held
cards.body:
Valerian's son Gallienus ruled alone from AD 260 to 268, while invaders and rebels tore at the empire. Gibbon paints a man of real gifts: an orator and poet, a gardener and cook, a friend of the philosopher Plotinus. When news came of lost provinces, he joked about whether Rome truly needed Egyptian linen or Gallic cloth. His talents went everywhere except to war and government, the two things the moment demanded.

Gibbon's verdict is one of his sharpest. Being clever and busy is not the same as doing what matters. When things are going wrong, the question is not what you are good at, but what your role needs from you right now.
cards.quote: a skilful gardener, an excellent cook, and most contemptible prince.
cards.locator: Chapter X: Emperors Decius, Gallus, Æmilianus, Valerian And Gallienus.—Part IV ¶37
cards.apply_it: List what you did yesterday. Circle the items that your most important role actually required. Tomorrow, start with one of those.

quiz.question: Which philosopher did Gallienus spend time with while crises mounted?
quiz.explanation: Gibbon says that when emergencies required him, Gallienus was often in conversation with Plotinus or busy with trifles.

cards.title: In the third-century crisis, war, famine and plague fed one another
cards.body:
Gibbon calls the twenty years after AD 248 a time of shame and misfortune, with emperors murdered, provinces invaded and rebels everywhere. War wrecked harvests, famine followed, and disease came after famine. A plague, he writes, raged from AD 250 to 265 in almost every province, city and household; at one point five thousand people were said to die each day in Rome.

He found a grim clue in Alexandria's lists of citizens entitled to free grain, which suggested more than half the city had died, though he treats wider estimates only as a suspicion. Crises rarely come singly. That is why steady institutions, and steady neighbours, matter most when everything is under strain.
cards.quote: During some time five thousand persons died daily in Rome; and many towns, that had escaped the hands of the Barbarians, were entirely depopulated.
cards.locator: Chapter X: Emperors Decius, Gallus, Æmilianus, Valerian And Gallienus.—Part IV ¶81
cards.apply_it: Think of one neighbour or relative who would struggle in a crisis. Make sure you have their number and they have yours.

quiz.question: What evidence suggested that more than half of Alexandria's people had died?
options: The register of citizens entitled to the grain distribution
quiz.explanation: Comparing the corn register before and after the reign of Gallienus showed the city's population had fallen by more than half.

cards.title: Zenobia of Palmyra ruled the East with a cool and steady head
cards.body:
Palmyra was a rich caravan city in the Syrian desert. Its leader Odenathus beat back the Persians and held the Roman East together after Valerian's capture, with his wife Zenobia often riding beside him. When he was murdered, she took over. She ruled Palmyra, Syria and the East for more than five years, added Egypt, and was courted by Arabia, Armenia and Persia. Gibbon praises her judgement: she could forgive when that was wise and punish when that was needed. Her careful spending was called stinginess, yet she was generous when it counted.

Her title, Queen of the East, eventually drew Aurelian against her. Her way of ruling still teaches: match your response to the situation, not to your mood.
cards.quote: If it was expedient to pardon, she could calm her resentment; if it was necessary to punish, she could impose silence on the voice of pity.
cards.locator: Chapter XI: Reign Of Claudius, Defeat Of The Goths.—Part III ¶5
cards.apply_it: Next time you feel angry with someone, or sorry for them, pause and ask: what response does this situation actually call for?

quiz.question: Which rich kingdom did Zenobia add to her husband's lands?
quiz.explanation: Gibbon says she added her ancestral inheritance, the populous and fertile kingdom of Egypt, to the dominions of Odenathus.

cards.title: Aurelian's soldiers obeyed him because he lived by his own rules
cards.body:
Aurelian, a soldier from the Danube provinces, ruled from AD 270 to 275. In under five years he ended the Gothic war, drove back invaders from Italy, recovered Gaul, Spain and Britain from a breakaway ruler, and overthrew Zenobia's eastern realm. Gibbon credits his strict discipline. Soldiers were forbidden to gamble, drink to excess or steal even a sheep, a chicken or a bunch of grapes from the people they lodged with. Their wages were enough, he wrote; wealth should come from the enemy, not from the tears of the provinces.

His punishments were brutal, and Gibbon calls them cruel. But the deeper reason he was obeyed was that he kept his own laws. Rules land differently when the person setting them visibly keeps them too.
cards.quote: His own conduct gave a sanction to his laws, and the seditious legions dreaded a chief who had learned to obey, and who was worthy to command.
cards.locator: Chapter XI: Reign Of Claudius, Defeat Of The Goths.—Part I ¶39
cards.apply_it: Pick one rule you expect others to follow. For the next week, keep it more strictly yourself than you ask them to.

quiz.question: According to Gibbon, why did the legions respect Aurelian?
options: His own conduct matched the laws he set
He came from a noble family
quiz.explanation: His conduct gave sanction to his laws: he had learned to obey before he commanded.

cards.title: Aurelian's attempt to restore honest coinage met with a bloody revolt
cards.body:
Debasing the coinage, Gibbon notes, suited the careless rule of Gallienus. Aurelian set out to restore honest money, and in Rome the mint workers rose in revolt. Aurelian wrote in a letter that seven thousand of his soldiers died putting it down. Other ancient writers say the moneyers had been adulterating the coins, and that the emperor restored public trust by exchanging good money for bad.

Gibbon doubts that mint workers alone could start a civil war and suspects wider opposition in Rome. But he explains why sound money is worth its brief pain: the loss is spread across many and soon forgotten, while the benefit lasts. Money that quietly loses value robs savers; fixing it is hard, but it pays off.
cards.quote: The transient evil is soon obliterated by the permanent benefit, the loss is divided among multitudes
cards.locator: Chapter XI: Reign Of Claudius, Defeat Of The Goths.—Part III ¶51
cards.apply_it: Compare what your savings earn with current inflation. If they are quietly losing value, look into one way to protect them.

quiz.question: According to the ancient writers, how did Aurelian restore public credit?
options: By exchanging good money for the bad
quiz.explanation: People were told to bring the debased coins to the treasury, where good money was given in exchange.

cards.title: Aurelian let his defeated rivals live in comfort instead of executing them
cards.body:
In AD 274 Aurelian held a magnificent triumph in Rome, parading Zenobia and Tetricus, who had ruled a breakaway empire in Gaul. Ancient conquerors often had such captives strangled once the parade was over. Aurelian did not. He gave Zenobia a villa at Tivoli, near Rome, where she lived as a Roman lady and her daughters married into noble families. Tetricus got back his rank and became governor of a region of southern Italy, and Aurelian teased him: wasn't that better than reigning beyond the Alps?

Gibbon does not hide that some of Zenobia's advisers had been executed. Still, generous terms for the leaders turned enemies into loyal subjects. Leaving the defeated a dignified future can end a conflict for good.
cards.quote: These usurpers, whom their defeat had convicted of the crime of treason, were permitted to spend their lives in affluence and honorable repose.
cards.locator: Chapter XI: Reign Of Claudius, Defeat Of The Goths.—Part III ¶39
cards.apply_it: Think of someone you beat in an argument or contest. Find one way to help them save face or move forward.

quiz.question: What did Aurelian give Zenobia after his triumph?
options: A villa at Tivoli near Rome
quiz.explanation: She settled at Tibur (Tivoli) as a Roman matron, and her descendants were still living in the fifth century.

cards.title: After Aurelian's murder, the empire ran for eight months without an emperor
cards.body:
In AD 275 Aurelian was killed by officers tricked with a forged death list. What followed, Gibbon says, is one of the best attested but most improbable events in history. The ashamed army asked the senate to choose an emperor; the senate asked the army; and the polite refusals went back and forth for about eight months. Officials simply carried on with their work, and the empire ran without a ruler, a usurper or a revolt.

At last the senate chose one of its own, the elderly Tacitus. He died after about six months on campaign, worn out by soldiers he could not control. The interregnum showed that sound habits and institutions can carry a state for a while even when no one is at the top.
cards.quote: an amazing period of tranquil anarchy, during which the Roman world remained without a sovereign, without a usurper, and without a sedition.
cards.locator: Chapter XII: Reigns Of Tacitus, Probus, Carus And His Sons.—Part I ¶5
cards.apply_it: If you were away for a month, what would keep running without you? Pick one process and write down how it works.

quiz.question: Who finally chose Tacitus as emperor?
quiz.explanation: After months of each side deferring to the other, the senate named Tacitus, one of its own members.

cards.title: Probus kept his soldiers busy with useful work, then pushed them too far
cards.body:
Probus, emperor from AD 276 to 282, came from the Danube provinces like Aurelian. Rather than leave his legions idle, he set them to work: improving navigation on the Nile in Egypt, building temples and porticoes, and planting vineyards on the hills of Gaul and Pannonia. Gibbon thinks such an army was perhaps the most useful body of people in the empire. But Probus overdid it, and he spoke of a day when peace would make a standing army unnecessary. In the heat of summer, while draining marshes near Sirmium, in today's Serbia, the exhausted soldiers mutinied and killed him. They regretted it at once.

Good intentions do not make a burden lighter. Check how a plan feels to those carrying it.
cards.quote: in the prosecution of a favorite scheme, the best of men, satisfied with the rectitude of their intentions, are subject to forget the bounds of moderation
cards.locator: Chapter XII: Reigns Of Tacitus, Probus, Carus And His Sons.—Part II ¶43
cards.apply_it: Ask one person who works with you how their load feels right now, and listen without defending the plan.

quiz.question: What were Probus's soldiers doing when they mutinied?
quiz.explanation: Forced to drain the unhealthy marshes in the summer heat, the soldiers threw down their tools and killed him.

cards.title: Diocletian, the son of slaves, rebuilt the empire with skill rather than glamour
cards.body:
Diocletian came from Dalmatia, on the coast of modern Croatia. Gibbon says his parents had been slaves in a senator's household. He rose through the army to command the palace guards, and in AD 284 the troops made him emperor. Gibbon judges his talents useful rather than dazzling: a strong mind sharpened by experience, skill in business, a balance of generosity and thrift, of mildness and firmness, and the patience to hold his aims steady while changing his methods.

Like Augustus, he was a statesman more than a warrior and used force only when policy failed. Steady competence and self-control carried him from the bottom of Roman society to the top.
cards.quote: His abilities were useful rather than splendid
cards.locator: Chapter XIII: Reign Of Diocletian And His Three Associates.—Part I ¶2
cards.apply_it: Name one 'useful rather than splendid' strength you have, such as reliability or patience. Use it deliberately on a problem this week.

quiz.question: How did Gibbon describe Diocletian's abilities?
quiz.explanation: Gibbon praises his practical gifts: experience, skill in business, and control of his own passions.

cards.title: Diocletian shared the empire among four rulers who worked in harmony
cards.body:
Diocletian saw that one man could not defend an empire attacked on every side. He made his comrade Maximian co-emperor, and some years later added two junior partners, the Caesars Galerius and Constantius. Each took a region: Constantius held Gaul, Spain and Britain; Galerius the Danube; Maximian Italy and Africa; and Diocletian the East. Marriages tied the families together. For years there was no jealousy among them, and their unity was compared to a choir led by a master.

The arrangement worked because each partner had a clear area and all accepted one leader's direction. Sharing a heavy load beats carrying it alone, as long as everyone knows what is theirs.
cards.quote: the singular happiness of their union has been compared to a chorus of music, whose harmony was regulated and maintained by the skilful hand of the first artist.
cards.locator: Chapter XIII: Reign Of Diocletian And His Three Associates.—Part I ¶14
cards.apply_it: Write down one responsibility you could hand to someone else, with a clear boundary of what is theirs to decide.

quiz.question: Which region did Constantius govern under Diocletian's system?
quiz.explanation: Constantius defended the West; Galerius held the Danube, Maximian Italy and Africa, and Diocletian the East.

cards.title: Four courts and a swollen bureaucracy meant heavier taxes for everyone
cards.body:
Diocletian's system had a price. Instead of one modest household like those of Augustus and Trajan, there were now three or four splendid courts, each competing in display. Ministers, magistrates and officials multiplied. A writer of the time complained that those who received now outnumbered those who paid. From then on, Gibbon says, writers of every party complained about the land tax and the poll tax.

Gibbon is fair to Diocletian: in his own reign the burden stayed within bounds and the treasury was well run. His fault was setting a precedent that others abused. Any organisation that adds layers faster than it adds producers will end up squeezing the people who do the work.
cards.quote: when the proportion of those who received exceeded the proportion of those who contributed, the provinces were oppressed by the weight of tributes.
cards.locator: Chapter XIII: Reign Of Diocletian And His Three Associates.—Part IV ¶11
cards.apply_it: Look at a group you belong to, at work or in a club. Are there more people managing than doing? Suggest one layer that could go.

quiz.question: What was Gibbon's main criticism of Diocletian on taxes?
options: He set precedents that later rulers abused
quiz.explanation: Gibbon says Diocletian deserves blame for pernicious precedents rather than actual oppression, and his revenues were managed with economy.

cards.title: Diocletian gave up the throne to grow cabbages and refused to go back
cards.body:
On 1 May AD 305, after twenty-one years in power, Diocletian did something no Roman emperor had done before: he resigned. He retired to his palace at Salona, near modern Split in Croatia, and filled his days with building, planting and gardening. When his old colleague Maximian urged him to take power again, Diocletian smiled and said that if Maximian could see the cabbages he had grown with his own hands, he would stop asking.

Gibbon notes that his retirement was not untroubled, as he watched the empire slide into conflict. Still, he knew when enough was enough. Stepping away from status for a simpler life can take more strength than holding on.
cards.quote: if he could show Maximian the cabbages which he had planted with his own hands at Salona, he should no longer be urged to relinquish the enjoyment of happiness for the pursuit of power.
cards.locator: Chapter XIII: Reign Of Diocletian And His Three Associates.—Part IV ¶24
cards.apply_it: Name one thing you chase for status rather than happiness. What simple pleasure could you give that time to instead?

quiz.question: Where did Diocletian spend his retirement?
quiz.explanation: He retired to his native Dalmatia, near modern Split, where he grew vegetables and built his great palace.

cards.title: Diocletian warned that a secluded ruler sees only through other people's eyes
cards.body:
In retirement Diocletian often told friends that ruling was the hardest of all arts. A few ministers, he explained, could combine to deceive their master. Raised above everyone, the ruler never heard the truth directly. He saw only what they showed him and heard only their version, so he gave important posts to the weak and corrupt and disgraced the best people. Even the wisest princes, he said, could be sold by their courtiers.

The irony is that Diocletian himself had made emperors harder to approach, with new ceremonies and guarded halls. Anyone with authority faces this risk. Without unfiltered views from every level, you end up managing a story instead of reality.
cards.quote: Secluded from mankind by his exalted dignity, the truth is concealed from his knowledge; he can see only with their eyes, he hears nothing but their misrepresentations.
cards.locator: Chapter XIII: Reign Of Diocletian And His Three Associates.—Part IV ¶24
cards.apply_it: This week, ask someone with no stake in pleasing you how a project or decision really looks from where they sit.

quiz.question: According to Diocletian, what was the most difficult of all arts?
quiz.explanation: He spoke of it with a warmth that, Gibbon says, could only come from experience.

cards.title: Diocletian's careful system fell apart soon after he stepped down
cards.body:
Diocletian's plan was that the two senior emperors would retire, the two Caesars would move up, and new Caesars would be chosen on merit. It worked while he was there to hold it together. Gibbon explains why it could not last: it needed two senior emperors without jealousy, two juniors without ambition, and four independent rulers all pursuing the same goal. After the abdications of AD 305 came eighteen years of discord and five civil wars, with rival rulers raising armies and taxes against each other.

A system that only works if everyone behaves unusually well is fragile. Good designs assume ordinary ambition and include ways to handle it.
cards.quote: two emperors without jealousy, two Cæsars without ambition, and the same general interest invariably pursued by four independent princes.
cards.locator: Chapter XIV: Six Emperors At The Same Time, Reunion Of The Empire.—Part I ¶2
cards.apply_it: Look at a plan you depend on. Does it only work if everyone behaves perfectly? Add one safeguard for when they don't.

quiz.question: How long did discord last after Diocletian's abdication, according to Gibbon?
quiz.explanation: The abdication was followed by eighteen years of discord and five civil wars.

cards.title: At York in AD 306, Constantine seized power because waiting was riskier
cards.body:
Constantine was the son of the emperor Constantius and Helena, whom Gibbon calls an innkeeper's daughter. As a young officer he served at the eastern court, where the senior emperor Galerius was jealous of him and kept delaying his departure. Constantine finally rode west to join his father in Britain. When Constantius died at York in AD 306, the western army proclaimed Constantine emperor. Gibbon thinks his show of reluctance was staged and that supporters had prepared the troops.

But Gibbon also names the reality: Galerius was hostile, and to survive, Constantine had to rule. Sometimes the safe-looking option, waiting, is the dangerous one. Weigh the cost of not acting as carefully as the cost of acting.
cards.quote: if he wished to live he must determine to reign.
cards.locator: Chapter XIV: Six Emperors At The Same Time, Reunion Of The Empire.—Part I ¶24
cards.apply_it: Think of a decision you keep putting off. Write down what waiting could cost you, then set a date to decide.

quiz.question: Where was Constantine proclaimed emperor?
quiz.explanation: His father Constantius died at York, and the western army there saluted Constantine as emperor.

cards.title: Constantine deliberated carefully, then struck fast at the Milvian Bridge
cards.body:
Maxentius, who held Rome and Italy, ruled harshly and was preparing to invade Gaul. Constantine at first tried negotiation, Gibbon says. Once convinced that war was unavoidable, he moved fast, overruled his timid advisers and crossed the Alps into Italy in AD 312. He feared Maxentius would shut himself inside Rome's walls. Instead Maxentius came out to fight just north of the city. Constantine led his cavalry in person, the enemy broke, and thousands drowned in the Tiber, Maxentius among them as he fled across the Milvian Bridge.

The pattern is worth copying. Take time to think before committing, but once committed, act with speed and energy.
cards.quote: He had deliberated with caution, he acted with vigor.
cards.locator: Chapter XIV: Six Emperors At The Same Time, Reunion Of The Empire.—Part II ¶36
cards.apply_it: Give yourself a deadline to decide one open question. Once decided, take the first concrete step within twenty-four hours.

quiz.question: How did Maxentius die?
options: He was killed by his own guards
He was forced into the Tiber and drowned
quiz.explanation: Crowds on the narrow Milvian Bridge pushed him into the river, where the weight of his armour drowned him.

cards.title: After victory, Constantine refused the crowd's demand for more executions
cards.body:
Gibbon judges Constantine's conduct after his victory in AD 312 as neither especially merciful nor excessively harsh. He had Maxentius's young sons and family put to death, as he would have expected for his own in defeat. But when the Roman crowd loudly demanded more victims, he resisted. Informers were punished, the innocent were recalled from exile and given back their property, and a general amnesty settled people's minds in Italy and Africa.

Gibbon is less impressed by Constantine's triumphal arch, partly decorated with sculpture taken from Trajan's monuments. But the amnesty mattered. After a bitter conflict, people need a clear signal that the reckoning is over.
cards.quote: A general act of oblivion quieted the minds and settled the property of the people, both in Italy and in Africa.
cards.locator: Chapter XIV: Six Emperors At The Same Time, Reunion Of The Empire.—Part III ¶23
cards.apply_it: If an old dispute still hangs over your team or family, say clearly that it is settled and you will not raise it again.

quiz.question: What did Constantine do when the crowd demanded more executions?
options: He left it to the senate
He resisted and declared a general amnesty
quiz.explanation: He punished informers, recalled exiles and passed a general act of oblivion.

cards.title: Constantine turned a one-off 'free gift' into a permanent tax
cards.body:
After his victory in AD 312, Constantine abolished the Praetorian Guard for good, ending the troops who had made and unmade emperors for three centuries. But Gibbon points out an irony. The Romans had backed Maxentius partly to escape a new tax. Maxentius then squeezed the senators for a so-called free gift, and they begged Constantine to rescue them. He defeated Maxentius and made the free gift a permanent tax, graded by wealth: eight, four or two pounds of gold a year, with even poor senators charged.

Charges introduced as exceptional tend to become permanent once someone finds them useful. When a one-off payment appears, ask what will stop it from becoming routine.
cards.quote: He vanquished the tyrant, and converted the free gift into a perpetual tax.
cards.locator: Chapter XIV: Six Emperors At The Same Time, Reunion Of The Empire.—Part III ¶28
cards.apply_it: Review your subscriptions and regular payments. Cancel one that began as a trial or one-time charge.

quiz.question: What did Constantine do with the senators' 'free gift'?
options: He made it a permanent tax
He handed it to the army
quiz.explanation: Senators were divided into classes paying eight, four or two pounds of gold a year.

cards.title: Gibbon gave five human reasons why early Christianity spread so fast
cards.body:
Gibbon's fifteenth chapter asks how Christianity, a small movement in the first century AD, spread across the empire. He sets aside the believer's answer, the truth of the faith and divine providence, saying he will examine only secondary, human causes. He names five: the firm zeal of believers; the hope of life after death; the miraculous powers credited to the early church; the pure and austere morals of its members; and its unity and organisation, which formed a growing community within the empire.

His tone is sceptical in places and has long been criticised, including by the editors of this very edition. But his question fits any movement: conviction, hope, moral example and strong community draw people in.
cards.quote: we may still be permitted, though with becoming submission, to ask, not indeed what were the first, but what were the secondary causes of the rapid growth of the Christian church.
cards.locator: Chapter XV: Progress Of The Christian Religion.—Part I ¶6
cards.apply_it: Think of a community you value. Which draws you most: shared conviction, hope, example, belonging or good organisation?

quiz.question: Which of these was NOT one of Gibbon's five causes?
options: The doctrine of a future life
The pure and austere morals of believers
The union and discipline of the church
quiz.explanation: His five causes were zeal, the hope of a future life, miraculous powers, pure morals, and unity and discipline.

cards.title: Early Christian communities cared for the poor, the sick and strangers
cards.body:
Gibbon describes how early Christian congregations pooled their money. Members gave voluntary offerings to a common fund. After modest support for the clergy and worship, the rest was, in his words, the sacred patrimony of the poor. It supported widows and orphans, the disabled, the sick and the elderly, welcomed strangers and helped prisoners. Richer churches sent aid to poorer ones in distant provinces, and abandoned infants were often taken in and raised.

The help went to people because they were in need, not because they had earned it. Gibbon notes that pagans who mocked the doctrines still acknowledged the kindness, and that it drew many in. Practical care has always been one of belief's most persuasive voices.
cards.quote: Such an institution, which paid less regard to the merit than to the distress of the object, very materially conduced to the progress of Christianity.
cards.locator: Chapter XV: Progress Of The Christian Religion.—Part VII ¶13
cards.apply_it: This week, give some time or money to someone in need without asking whether they have earned it.

quiz.question: According to Gibbon, how did kindly pagans view Christian charity?
options: They mocked the doctrines but acknowledged the benevolence
quiz.explanation: Pagans moved by humanity derided the doctrines but acknowledged the benevolence of the new sect.
